claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a retained FCC matrix.
The starting alloy exhibits high strength.
The starting alloy exhibits good fatigue performance.
Elevated-temperature degradation in oxidizing environments is governed by selective and synergistic oxidation of Cr, Ti, and, to a lesser extent, Al.
Cr, Ti, and Al diffuse at different rates in the alloy during elevated-temperature exposure.
Differential diffusion and oxygen affinities cause discrete oxide islands to nucleate instead of a continuous protective scale.
The discrete oxide islands form predominantly at or along grain boundaries.
The principal oxide phases are Cr2O3 and TiO2.
The non-uniform oxide islands compromise surface integrity.
The bulk FCC matrix remains intact while heterogeneous surface oxidation develops.
A trace Nb addition will slow the diffusion of Cr, Ti, and Al.
Slower reactive-element diffusion caused by Nb will delay the onset of heterogeneous oxidation.
Slower reactive-element diffusion caused by Nb will reduce the severity of heterogeneous oxidation.
The Nb-modified alloy will develop a more uniform and potentially more protective oxide layer than the baseline alloy.
A suitably controlled trace Nb addition can modify oxidation kinetics without altering phase stability or mechanical integrity.
Under reducing H2/Ar conditions, oxidation will be minimal relative to oxidizing conditions.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply from 700 to 900 degrees Celsius and at oxygen partial pressures from 0.2 to 1 atm.
Outside the stated temperature and oxygen-pressure boundaries, phase-stability changes or different oxidation kinetics may produce alternative degradation mechanisms.
Formation of a continuous, uniform oxide scale in the oxidized baseline alloy without discrete islands would falsify the proposed heterogeneous-oxidation mechanism.
Failure of the Nb-modified samples to show delayed or altered oxidation relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed Nb-mediated diffusion effect.
